title: What Does the Bible Say About Wealth and the Poor?
subtitle: Scripture speaks about wealth and the poor with a frequency our preaching has never matched. Both parties found a way to keep the texts and lose the cost.

sections.title: A Subject We Cannot Avoid, Avoided
sections.body:
Open a concordance and count. Scripture returns to money, possessions, and the poor hundreds of times. Jesus talked about wealth again and again, and a large share of his parables touch money. The Torah legislates it, the prophets rage over it, and the epistles warn about it in their closing chapters like a recurring emergency.

Now count the sermons. Pastors, and I am one, preach the money texts at a rate that bears no relation to their frequency in the book we claim as our authority. Most of us aren't censoring anything on purpose. We've just learned, the way a child learns a dialect, which passages are for preaching and which are for footnotes, and so have congregations, red and blue alike.

Craig Blomberg's survey of the whole canon concludes that neither poverty nor riches is the biblical ideal, but that surplus sitting beside need is treated, page after page, as a spiritual crisis. We've learned not to see those pages, and both tribes did the unlearning, by different methods that are worth a close look.

sections.title: Jubilee, Gleaning, and the Lord's Land
sections.body:
Israel's law built an economy for neighbors. Every seventh year, debts released, Deuteronomy 15. Every fiftieth, Jubilee: land returned to families so that no permanent underclass could form, liberty proclaimed throughout the land, Leviticus 25. Harvest edges left standing so the poor and the immigrant could glean with dignity, working rather than begging, Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24. Wages were paid before sundown, and no interest was charged on loans to the poor.

Christopher Wright insists this was the economy itself, a built structure of obligation, rather than charity bolted onto one, because the land was the Lord's and Israel were tenants on it. The whole system assumed the thing we deny, that my harvest isn't entirely mine.

Then come the prophets, sent when the system was strangled by the people it inconvenienced. Amos on the cows of Bashan and the scales rigged against the needy. Isaiah on those who join house to house and field to field until no room remains. Isaiah 58 on the fast God refuses while workers go unpaid. The charge was almost never that Israel had stopped believing; it was that Israel kept worshiping while the gleaning fields quietly disappeared. The liturgy outlived the obedience, as it usually does.

sections.title: Luke's Woes and James's Howl
sections.body:
The New Testament does not soften any of this. Luke's Jesus blesses the poor and then turns to the other side of the crowd: woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. He tells of a rich fool whose new barns outlived him by one night, and of a rich man whose only recorded crime was stepping over Lazarus at his gate until the day they both died. Zacchaeus is saved and half his goods leave the house that same afternoon, and Jesus calls the giving the evidence of the salvation, not its price.

James writes to Christian congregations the way Amos wrote to Samaria: come now, you rich, weep and howl. The wages you withheld are crying out, and the cries have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. Paul tells Timothy that those who desire to be rich fall into a snare, and then instructs the wealthy, note that he assumes the church contains them, to be rich in good works and generous instead.

None of these texts is obscure, and every one of them sits in the lectionary. We've all read them, recently, and they've cost most of us, me included, almost nothing. Something has to explain that.

sections.title: Spiritualize or Outsource
sections.body:
What explains it is that American Christians built two escape routes, one per party, and both of them work.

The right spiritualizes. Blessed are the poor in spirit, the reading goes, so the poverty texts are about humility. Jubilee is fulfilled in Christ, so it asks nothing of my ledger. The rich young ruler was a special case, his problem was attachment, and since I judge my own heart unattached, I may keep everything. Money becomes a heart issue, and the heart, conveniently, is invisible.

The left outsources. The texts are about systems, so my obligation is a policy preference. I advocate the right programs, vote the right way, and the state does my gleaning for me, while my own giving stays exactly where it was. Compassion becomes a position, and positions are free.

Both moves are built from real truths, which is why they work. Wealth is a heart issue, and justice does involve systems. But watch how it comes out. In both cases the text is affirmed and the wallet goes untouched, two theologies with one bank statement. Many of us have believed the first escape and voted the second, and neither one ever asked us for a key to the house.

sections.title: A Person, a Congregation, a Ledger
sections.body:
What do the money texts actually ask?

Of a person they ask that giving be proportionate, planned, and felt. Zacchaeus set a number out loud. The Macedonian churches gave beyond their means and Paul praised them for it rather than correcting them. Tim Keller argues from these texts that generosity in Scripture is not a tip added to a comfortable life but a structural feature of a converted one. So the question worth asking is whether my giving has ever altered how I live, and many of us, pastors included, would have to answer no.

Of a congregation they ask that the church be the first economy where Jubilee is visible. Acts reports that there was no needy person among them, an echo of Deuteronomy 15 that Luke surely intended. A church budget is a confession of faith, and so is a personal one. Many of ours confess that we believe in Jesus and trust the mortgage.

The texts won't be argued away. They can only be obeyed or avoided, and we have grown skilled at avoidance, left and right, each tribe watching the other's hypocrisy with perfect vision. Somewhere in your city tonight is a Lazarus whose name God knows. The text is waiting to find out whether you do.
